performers: Barbara Schubert, the DuPage Symphony Orchestra
intro: Urlicht (Sehr feierlich, aber schlicht), the fourth movement of the Symphony No. 2 “Resurrection”, follows three movements of marches and dances, and here an alto sings the symphony’s first words. The text is a short prayer in which even an angel cannot turn the traveller away from God.

sections.label: A · Alto and brass chorale
sections.mNote: One voice, answered by a hymn for brass

sections.label: B · Alto solo on suffering
sections.mNote: The vocal line rises through chromatic harmony.

sections.label: C · Angel episode, clarinet and violin
sections.mNote: Clarinet and solo violin accompany the account of the angel

sections.label: B′ · Rising phrases, cadence in D♭
sections.mNote: Rising phrases over tremolo strings, then a cadence in D♭

cues.title: Alto entry and brass chorale
cues.text: An alto begins alone, with “O Röschen roth!” in long, held notes. Trumpets and horns follow with a hymn. Mahler marks the song Sehr feierlich, aber schlicht (very solemn, yet simple) and adds Choralmässig, in the manner of a chorale.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 2, Hofmeister full score (1897), movement IV, p. 128: attacca from the third movement; Sehr feierlich, aber schlicht (Choralmässig), Nicht schleppen; the alto’s “O Röschen roth!” with fermatas, then trumpets and horns in chorale texture over muted strings, and a note that the brass should stand together at the back of the orchestra. Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide: the first line of text opens the movement, followed by a chorale-like passage for a brass choir that Mahler asks to sit at the rear of the orchestra: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Brass chorale, rising theme
cues.text: The brass chorale moves in rising steps. An expanded version of this ascending theme returns in the finale as the resurrection theme.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation page on the movement says a solemn chorale, gently stated on the brass, affirms the innocent faith of childhood, and that an expanded version of this ascending theme becomes the final movement’s resurrection theme: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-4-lied-1-urlicht-sehr-feierlich-aber-schlicht/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Alto, “Der Mensch liegt in größter Noth!”
cues.text: The alto sings “Der Mensch liegt in größter Noth! Der Mensch liegt in größter Pein!” The vocal line takes on chromatic notes, and the metre keeps changing. At “Je lieber möcht’ ich im Himmel sein” (I would rather be in heaven), Mahler marks a ritenuto and molto espress.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement IV, p. 129 (IMSLP #415748): the alto’s “Der Mensch liegt in größter Noth! Der Mensch liegt in größter Pein!” over low strings and horns, the bar lengths changing, then “Je lieber möcht’ ich im Himmel sein” with rit. and molto espress.: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/e2/IMSLP415748-PMLP49406-GMahler_Symphony_No.2_fe_UE_reprint_RSL1.pdf . Bettie Jo Basinger, Utah Symphony guide: chromaticism infiltrates the vocal line, which gradually rises and constantly fluctuates in metre: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Orchestral manuscript, Steinbach, 1893
cues.text: Mahler dated an orchestral manuscript of Urlicht at Steinbach am Attersee on 19 July 1893. That summer he was also working on the dance movements of the Second Symphony. The song already existed before he decided to place it in the symphony.
cues.evidence: The dated manuscript is Zweig MS 49, folio 6r. Mahler’s 1895 letter to Hermann Behn establishes that the song preceded the decision to include it: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-4-lied-1-urlicht-sehr-feierlich-aber-schlicht/

cues.title: Source of the text, 1808
cues.text: Urlicht is a folk poem from Des Knaben Wunderhorn. It was printed in the second volume (Heidelberg, 1808) under the heading Mündlich, meaning by word of mouth. Mahler repeats several lines, among them “Ach nein, ich liess mich nicht abweisen.”
cues.evidence: Paul Banks’s Mahler catalogue prints the text from Des Knaben Wunderhorn, vol. II (Heidelberg, 1808), p. 11, headed Mündlich, beside Mahler’s version with its repeated lines: https://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/Symph2/Texts.htm

cues.title: Central section, Etwas bewegter
cues.text: At Etwas bewegter the music turns to the minor. A clarinet figure, harp notes and a glockenspiel stroke mark the time as the traveller meets an angel. A solo violin plays a longer melody, and three sharps appear in the signature as the angel tries to turn the traveller back.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement IV, pp. 130–131 (IMSLP #415748): Etwas bewegter at rehearsal 3 with five flats, a clarinet figure p deutlich with harp and glockenspiel, a solo violin marked ohne Dämpfer at “Da kam ich auf einen breiten Weg”, then three sharps at “da kam ein Engelein und wollt’ mich abweisen”: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/e2/IMSLP415748-PMLP49406-GMahler_Symphony_No.2_fe_UE_reprint_RSL1.pdf . Bettie Jo Basinger, Utah Symphony guide: the central section begins in a minor key; clarinet, harp and glockenspiel mark off regular increments of time as the voice sings lines five to seven slightly quicker, with solo violin and flute prominent: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: “Ach nein!”, leidenschaftlich
cues.text: Mahler marks the line “Ach nein! Ich liess mich nicht abweisen.” leidenschaftlich, passionately, over string tremolo. “Ich bin von Gott, ich will wieder zu Gott” is marked zart drängend (gently urging). The phrases then rise with growing expression.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement IV, pp. 131–132 (IMSLP #415748): Leidenschaftlich at “Ach nein! Ich ließ mich nicht abweisen” over string tremolo; zart drängend at “Ich bin von Gott und will wieder zu Gott”, then mit steigerndem Ausdruck. Bettie Jo Basinger, Utah Symphony guide: Mahler sets the eighth and ninth lines of the poem with a zart drängend figure: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing bars in D♭ major
cues.text: After the alto’s last word, “Leben”, the solo violins and strings continue in D♭ major with the harps. Mahler marks the ending gänzlich ersterbend, dying away completely, and writes at the foot of the page that the finale follows without a break.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement IV, p. 133 (IMSLP #415748): after the alto’s last words, “bis in das ewig selig Leben”, the solo violins and strings continue in D♭ major with the harps, marked gänzlich ersterbend; printed at the foot of the page: folgt ohne jede Unterbrechung der 5. Satz: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/e2/IMSLP415748-PMLP49406-GMahler_Symphony_No.2_fe_UE_reprint_RSL1.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Alto re-enters after brass chorale
transitions.how: The brass chorale closes in D♭ major, and the alto re-enters over strings. At the words about human suffering, semitones enter her melody and the metre changes frequently.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement IV, pp. 128–130. Bettie Jo Basinger, Utah Symphony guide: the brass choir’s chorale-like passage, then chromaticism infiltrating the vocal line: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide

transitions.title: Oboe turn, then clarinet figures
transitions.to: C · Angel episode, clarinet and violin
transitions.how: A solo oboe plays a turning phrase that closes the alto’s first section. The middle section begins in a minor key at a quicker tempo. Clarinet figures enter around the voice while harp and glockenspiel mark the time. A solo violin then extends these figures into a longer tune as the traveller tells of the angel.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement IV, pp. 129–131. Bettie Jo Basinger, Utah Symphony guide: a solo oboe closes the first portion; the central section begins in a minor key, with clarinet, harp and glockenspiel marking regular increments of time, a slightly quicker voice and a prominent solo violin: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide

transitions.title: Alto line rises through semitones
transitions.from: C · Angel episode, clarinet and violin
transitions.to: B′ · Rising phrases, cadence in D♭
transitions.how: After the middle section’s move into three sharps, the alto enters at “Ach nein!”, marked leidenschaftlich, over string tremolo. At “Ich bin von Gott” the phrases are marked zart drängend and mit steigerndem Ausdruck, and the line rises. The strings play the final D♭-major cadence after the singer’s last word.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement IV, pp. 131–133: Leidenschaftlich at “Ach nein!” over tremolo, zart drängend and mit steigerndem Ausdruck at “Ich bin von Gott”, and the strings’ D♭-major cadence after the last word. Bettie Jo Basinger, Utah Symphony guide: Mahler sets the eighth and ninth lines with a zart drängend figure: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 2, IV. Urlicht, full score (Hofmeister; Universal Edition reprint)
source.locator: Fourth movement, pp. 128–133, rehearsal figures 1–6: alto prayer, brass chorale, clarinet and solo-violin middle, and the closing string cadence.

timeline.note: The alto begins above muted strings; the brass answers with a chorale.
Trumpets and horns harmonise the chorale above bassoons, contrabassoon and the sustained bass.
The alto resumes over sustained string harmony after the brass chorale.
Soft trumpet phrases recalling earlier material answer the alto while the string harmony moves beneath the phrase.
The alto’s rising phrase gives way to an oboe turn over sustained strings.
Clarinet and solo violin accompany the traveller’s story, with harp notes and a glockenspiel stroke.
Piccolo doubles the ornamented violin line; harps and soft strings accompany the passage about the angel.
The alto sings the refusal over tremolo strings, harp chords, and soft horns and bassoons.
Wind and brass join the vocal climax before the slow closing phrase.
Clarinets and bassoons play quietly with the final vocal line; two harps play the closing harmony.
Muted divided strings complete the D♭-major cadence after the alto’s last word.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor.
